The Maestro, Season 2 · Part 3 · Phase 5 · 🧭 CEO hat

The Strategy One-Pager

Money and people are not a strategy. Before the new team starts building, Gopala writes one page that says where the company plays, how it wins, and what it will not do, against three kinds of competitor that are all larger: frontier labs shipping coding agents every few months, open-weight models with do-it-yourself harnesses, and developer-tool incumbents adding AI to products buyers already have. This part builds that page from 31 customer interviews, a scoring script with a sensitivity test that shows how narrow the lead is, a bottom-up market size, the moat in plain terms, three bets with kill criteria, and the list of things the company refuses to do.

1. Mission log: months 22–24

Week 92 · Interviews
  • Starts 31 interviews with buyers and users: current customers, lost deals and teams that never bought (scenario).
Week 95 · The scoring
  • Turns the interviews into weights; writes positioning.py; runs the sensitivity test.
Week 97 · The page
  • Drafts the one-pager; the board debates a broader "general coding agent" strategy and rejects it (section 13).
Week 98 · Shared
  • Reads the page to the whole company; every team writes its quarterly goals against it (S2 Part 4).

2. Strategy in one page: diagnosis, policy, actions

  • He uses Richard Rumelt's "kernel" of good strategy.
    • A diagnosis: what is really going on, and what is the hardest part.
    • A guiding policy: the overall approach to that hardest part.
    • Coherent actions: a few steps that reinforce each other.
    • Rumelt contrasts this with "bad strategy": goals dressed as strategy, fluff, and failing to face the main challenge.
  • The diagnosis, in one paragraph.
    • General coding agents from frontier labs are improving fast and are good enough for most code most of the time.
    • Buyers with private, regulated code still hesitate, not because the agents are weak but because they cannot show auditors why each change is safe.
    • Maestro's advantage is not a better general model; it is a model and a process that learn a customer's code under a gate that produces evidence.
  • The guiding policy.
    • Be the most trusted way to improve private, regulated codebases with AI, and let the general labs win the general market.
  • The coherent actions.
    • Sell to regulated mid-size companies first (section 8).
    • Invest in environments and the skill library, not in winning public benchmarks (Phase 6).
    • Make the gate's evidence part of the product (Phase 8).

3. The competition, in four groups

  • Frontier labs.
    • They ship coding and computer-use agents on a fast cadence. In October 2026 alone the site's tracker logged GPT-6.1 Terra (a cheaper computer-use model), Gemini 4 Argon reaching wide availability and Gemini 4 Carbon for security work, and Anthropic donating the Agent Skills standard to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation.
    • Strengths: model capability, distribution, money. Weakness for this market: one product for everyone, and limited ability to train on each customer's private code.
  • Open-weight models with a do-it-yourself harness.
    • Large open models such as Mistral Large 4 (weights released 29 October 2026) and Kimi K3.1 make it possible for a capable team to build its own agent.
    • Strengths: price and control. Weakness: the customer has to build and maintain evaluation, safety and the harness.
  • Developer-tool incumbents.
    • Code hosting, IDE and CI vendors add agents to products buyers already pay for.
    • Strengths: distribution and integration. Weakness: their agents are usually built on someone else's model and are general.
  • Other specialists.
    • Start-ups targeting one language, one industry or one task (tests, migrations, security fixes).
    • They are the likeliest acquirers or acquisition targets, and occasionally partners.

Four competitor groups and what they have that Maestro does not

🏛️Frontier labscapability, distribution
🧩Open model + DIYprice, control
🧰Tool incumbentsalready installed
🎯Specialistsfocus on one niche

The groups are archetypes, not ratings of named companies.

4. What 31 buyers said (scenario)

Scenario
  • The interviews, the people in them and every weight below are the story's. The method, top-three mentions turned into weights, is a simple and common way to summarise buyer interviews.
  • Who he talked to.
    • Nine current customers, eight lost deals, eight teams that never evaluated Maestro, six that built their own agent on an open model.
    • Each ranked their top three reasons for choosing an AI coding product, from a fixed list of six.
  • How he turned answers into weights.
    • A criterion's weight is the share of top-three mentions it received, normalised to 100%.
    • He reports the weights with the number of interviews, because 31 is small: one more interview can move a weight by a few points.

What buyers ranked in their top three (scenario weights)

Works on our private code24%
Evidence each change is safe20%
Raw model capability16%
Price per task14%
Fits our tools today14%
Vendor will exist in 3 years12%

The weights in positioning.py.

  • What surprised him.
    • Lost deals cited "vendor will exist in three years" more than price: a start-up's risk is a real cost to buyers.
    • Teams that built their own agent were the most interested in buying the evaluation and gate as a separate product (a seed for Phase 8's "harness as product").

5. Scoring the options

  • Each option gets a 1–5 score per criterion.
    • Scores are Gopala's judgement of each archetype, argued in a team review and written down with reasons.
    • Maestro scores low on "vendor will exist in three years" (2 of 5): honesty about the weakest point.
positioning.py · Python 3, no dependencies; scenario weights and scores
"""positioning.py — how four kinds of option score on what buyers said matters.

Weights come from the story's 31 SCENARIO customer interviews (share of
buyers who ranked the criterion in their top three, normalised). Scores
(1-5) are Gopala's own judgement of each archetype, not measurements of
any real company. The sensitivity test asks: how far must one weight move
before Maestro stops winning?
"""
CRIT = ["works on our private code", "evidence each change is safe", "raw model capability",
        "price per task", "fits our tools today", "vendor will exist in 3 years"]
W = [0.24, 0.20, 0.16, 0.14, 0.14, 0.12]
OPTS = {
    "Maestro (specialist)":        [5, 5, 3, 4, 3, 2],
    "frontier-lab coding agent":   [3, 3, 5, 3, 4, 5],
    "open model + DIY harness":    [4, 2, 3, 5, 2, 3],
    "dev-tool incumbent add-on":   [2, 3, 3, 3, 5, 5],
}

def score(w):
    return {k: sum(a * b for a, b in zip(w, v)) for k, v in OPTS.items()}

def main():
    s = score(W)
    for k, v in sorted(s.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1]):
        print(f"{k:28} {v:.2f}")
    print("sensitivity: weight increase (others shrink in proportion) that makes Maestro lose")
    for i, c in enumerate(CRIT):
        for step in range(1, 101):
            w = [x * (1 - step / 100) for x in W]
            w[i] = W[i] + (1 - W[i]) * step / 100
            w = [x / sum(w) for x in w]
            r = score(w)
            best = max(r, key=r.get)
            if best != "Maestro (specialist)":
                print(f"  {c:30} {W[i]:.2f} -> {w[i]:.2f}  {best} wins"); break
        else:
            print(f"  {c:30} never")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
$ python3 positioning.py # scenario interviews; archetype scores Maestro (specialist) 3.90 frontier-lab coding agent 3.70 dev-tool incumbent add-on 3.28 open model + DIY harness 3.18 sensitivity: weight increase (others shrink in proportion) that makes Maestro lose works on our private code never evidence each change is safe never raw model capability 0.16 -> 0.24 frontier-lab coding agent wins price per task 0.14 -> 0.50 open model + DIY harness wins fits our tools today 0.14 -> 0.29 frontier-lab coding agent wins vendor will exist in 3 years 0.12 -> 0.18 frontier-lab coding agent wins

Frontier-lab coding agent3.70
Dev-tool incumbent add-on3.28
Open model + DIY harness3.18

6. How narrow the lead is

  • Maestro wins, but by 0.20 points out of 5.
    • The sensitivity test raises one weight at a time (shrinking the others in proportion) until another option wins.
  • What flips it.
    • If raw model capability rises from 16% to 24% of what buyers care about, the frontier-lab agent wins.
    • If "vendor will exist in three years" rises from 12% to 18%, the frontier lab wins again.
    • If fitting existing tools rises from 14% to 29%, the same.
    • Only a huge rise in price sensitivity (14% to 50%) makes the do-it-yourself option win.
  • What never flips it.
    • More weight on working with private code, or on evidence that each change is safe. Those are the criteria to make more important to buyers.
  • The strategic reading.
    • The company must keep buyers' attention on private code and evidence, where it is strong, and close the gap on durability and tool fit, where it is weak.
    • It must not compete on raw capability: a few points of buyer attention there and the lead is gone.
Rule from the sensitivity test
  • Every product and marketing decision is checked against one question: does it make private-code results and change-by-change evidence matter more to buyers, or does it pull the comparison towards raw capability?

7. Try it: change what buyers care about

Positioning scores (our model, same numbers as positioning.py)

  • Things to try.
    • Push raw model capability to 25: the frontier lab takes the lead.
    • Push evidence each change is safe to 35: Maestro's lead roughly doubles.
    • Set price to 50 and everything else low: the do-it-yourself option wins, which is why Maestro does not sell to price-first buyers.

8. Where to play

  • Bottom-up, not top-down.
    • Investors distrust "1% of all developers" sizing. Gopala counts engineering teams he can actually reach, the share that fit (private code, regulated or security-sensitive) and a realistic price per team.
    • All inputs below are our assumptions for the story, labelled as such.
market_size.py · Python 3, no dependencies; all inputs are assumptions
"""market_size.py — bottom-up market sizing, the way investors check it.

Every input is OUR ASSUMPTION for the story (labelled on the page), not a
market statistic: we count teams Gopala can actually reach, not 'all developers'.
"""
SEGMENTS = [  # segment, companies, engineering teams each, share that fit (private code, regulated), $k per team per year
    ("regulated mid-size (finance, health)", 6000, 8, 0.30, 36),
    ("large enterprise", 1500, 60, 0.15, 30),
    ("software scale-ups", 12000, 4, 0.20, 24),
]
REACH_3Y = 0.04      # share of the fitting market a 40-person company can win in three years (assumption)

def main():
    tot = 0
    for name, n, teams, fit, price in SEGMENTS:
        v = n * teams * fit * price / 1000
        tot += v
        print(f"{name:38} {n * teams * fit:9,.0f} teams  ${v:7,.0f}M/yr")
    print(f"{'serviceable market':38} {'':15}  ${tot:7,.0f}M/yr")
    print(f"3-year target at {REACH_3Y:.0%} of it:            ${tot * REACH_3Y:7,.1f}M ARR")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
$ python3 market_size.py # our assumptions, not market statistics regulated mid-size (finance, health) 14,400 teams $ 518M/yr large enterprise 13,500 teams $ 405M/yr software scale-ups 9,600 teams $ 230M/yr serviceable market $ 1,154M/yr 3-year target at 4% of it: $ 46.2M ARR

Serviceable market by segment (our assumptions, $M a year)

🏦 Regulated mid-size · $518M14,400 fitting teams in finance and health, about $36k per team a year
🏢 Large enterprise · $405M13,500 fitting teams, about $30k per team
🚀 Software scale-ups · $230M9,600 fitting teams, about $24k per team

Real output of market_size.py; about $1.15B a year in total.

  • The choice.
    • Regulated mid-size companies first: the highest price per team, the strongest need for evidence, and sales cycles a small team can manage.
    • Large enterprises second, once security reviews and private deployments are ready (Phase 8).
    • Scale-ups opportunistically: they buy fast but care most about raw capability and price, where Maestro is weakest.
  • The three-year number.
    • Winning 4% of the serviceable market would be about $46M of ARR: a target to test, not a forecast.

9. How to win: the moat in plain words

  • Not the weights.
    • Open models catch up within months, and frontier labs spend more on one run than the whole Series A.
  • What compounds.
    • The skill library: verified skills from every customer task, kept per customer under the data agreements.
    • Environments: thousands of runnable task environments with checks, which are expensive to build and improve every model (Phase 6, Part 8).
    • The gate's record: years of approved and rejected updates with reasons, which auditors and buyers can inspect.
    • Integrations and trust with regulated customers, which take quarters to earn.
  • In Hamilton Helmer's "7 Powers" terms.
    • Switching costs: a customer's skills and evaluation history live in Maestro.
    • Process power: the gate and evaluation machinery are hard to copy quickly.
    • Counter-positioning: a general lab is unlikely to make every update wait for customer-specific evidence, because it would slow its own release cadence.

The flywheel that is the moat

🧑‍💻Customer taskreal work on private code
✅Verified skillchecked by tests and reviewers
🏗️Environmentturned into a runnable check
🚦Gate recordevery update with evidence
🤝Trustmore tasks shared

Each turn makes the next customer easier to win and harder to lose.

10. What we will not do

  • The list that makes the strategy real.
    • No general consumer coding assistant.
    • No competing on public coding leaderboards as a sales message.
    • No training on one customer's code for another customer's model.
    • No loosening the gate to match a competitor's release cadence.
    • No price war with open-model do-it-yourself teams.
    • No custom consulting projects that do not produce reusable skills or environments.
    • No exclusive deals with a single cloud provider (S2 Part 1).
  • Each item has a reason and an owner.
    • When a big deal tempts the company to break one, the owner writes why, and the board decides.

11. Three bets, each with a kill criterion

BetWhat would prove itKill criterion (by month 30)
Regulated mid-size is the beachhead20 customers in finance and health; NRR above 120% on the first two cohortsFewer than 8 new regulated customers by month 30
Environments are the next moatEach 1,000 new environments improves Maestro on held-out customer tasksNo measurable gain from two successive batches (Phase 6)
Evidence sellsBuyers cite the gate record as a top-three reason in win reviewsCited in fewer than a quarter of wins
  • Why kill criteria again.
    • Season 1, Part 1 wrote kill criteria for the idea; Season 2 writes them for the strategy. A bet without one is a hope.

12. The page itself

Maestro strategy, month 22 (one page)
  • Diagnosis.
    • General agents are good enough for most code; regulated teams cannot prove each change is safe.
  • Guiding policy.
    • The most trusted way to improve private, regulated codebases with AI.
  • Where we play.
    • Regulated mid-size first, then large enterprise; scale-ups opportunistically.
  • How we win.
    • Skills, environments and the gate's record; switching costs and process power.

13. The board debate (scenario)

Scenario
  • At the month-23 board meeting the Series A partner argues for a broader "general coding agent for every team", pointing at the market size. Gopala answers with the sensitivity test: in the general market, raw capability matters more, and that is where the lead disappears.
  • How it was settled.
    • The independent director asked for a test, not an argument: run both messages in parallel to 40 prospects for six weeks.
    • The specialist message converted about twice as often in the story's test; the board accepted the strategy with a review at month 30.
  • What Gopala conceded.
    • A self-serve trial for scale-ups, with no sales effort, to keep an eye on the general market.

14. What the strategy means for pricing

  • Price on the outcome the strategy emphasises.
    • Season 1's hybrid pricing (Part 16): a platform fee plus a price per accepted task. The strategy keeps it, because it ties revenue to work customers accept, not to tokens.
  • An evidence tier.
    • Regulated customers pay more for an audit package: the gate record for every update applied to their account, exportable for auditors.
    • It makes the strongest criterion in the interviews (evidence) visible on the price list.
  • No race to the bottom.
    • The sensitivity test said only extreme price sensitivity makes the do-it-yourself option win. Price-first buyers are not the target, so Maestro does not discount to win them.
  • The self-serve trial.
    • A limited free tier for scale-ups (section 13), capped by tasks per month, as a window on the general market rather than a revenue line.

15. Build, buy or partner

  • What Maestro builds itself.
    • The model and the self-improvement loop, the gate and evaluation machinery, the skill library and environments: everything on the moat list.
  • What it buys.
    • Compute, observability, identity and billing systems, sandboxes where a good product exists (see Agent Layer Part 2).
  • Where it partners.
    • Code hosting and CI vendors, for integrations and marketplace listings (Phase 9).
    • Systems integrators that serve regulated industries.
  • The open question for Phase 8.
    • Should customers be able to run Maestro's harness and gate with other labs' models? It could widen the market and weaken the model moat. The strategy leaves it open with a test date (S2 Part 17).

16. Strategy risks and early warnings

RiskEarly warningResponse
A frontier lab launches a private-code product with per-customer trainingCustomers ask for side-by-side trialsLean on the gate record and audit package; accelerate the evidence tier
An open model closes the capability gap at a fraction of the priceDo-it-yourself teams win more trialsPost-train the open base (Phase 7 option); sell the harness
Regulation makes evidence mandatoryAuditors ask for change recordsAn opportunity: the product already produces them
Incumbents bundle a good-enough agent freeLost deals cite "already have one"Deeper integrations; partner rather than fight
The beachhead is too smallFewer than 8 regulated wins by month 30 (kill criterion)Re-run market_size.py; move to large enterprise earlier
  • Who watches them.
    • Each risk has an owner and appears in the board's risk register every quarter (S2 Part 4).

17. Eight strategy mistakes

  • Writing goals ("be the leader") and calling them a strategy.
  • Choosing the biggest market instead of the one you can win.
  • Scoring yourself without scoring your weakest criterion honestly.
  • Ignoring the sensitivity test: a lead that one weight can erase is not a moat.
  • Treating model weights as the moat.
  • A "not do" list with no owner, broken by the first big deal.
  • Bets without kill criteria.
  • Sharing the strategy as a deck instead of one page everyone can quote.

20. The series

The Maestro, Season 2: 23 parts in five phases (Season 1: 18 parts)

VerdictThe strategy fits on one page because it is a set of choices: play where private code and evidence matter, win with skills, environments and the gate's record, and refuse the markets where raw capability decides. The scoring script shows the lead is real but narrow, which is the most useful thing it says. Next: the operating cadence that turns the page into weekly work.
